newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: China says its aviation is booming, seeks funds.
newsitem.headline: China says its aviation is booming, seeks funds.

text.p: China's aviation industry is booming with major expansions planned to handle growth in cargo and passenger traffic, and it is time for the West to relax its purse strings for funding, a senior official said on Friday

Hai Liancheng, finance chief at China's Civil Aviation Administration (CAAC), told a Geneva conference that his country expected to more than double its air fleet to 1,000 commercial aircraft by 2000.
China planned to order as many as 300 planes in the coming years, said Liancheng, although he did not specify the type of planes or whether the orders would be firm or involve options.
"Our industry has made progress but we still have a long way to go. The main focus is the shortage of funds," he said.
Liancheng said China was considering securitisation backed by aircraft mortgage and aircraft lease to finance orders.
"We hope to strengthen cooperation with our partners in short-term financing for greater flexibility," he said.
"We are also concerned about the financing of supplies and spare parts. All these require great support from friends in the finance circles and the aviation world."

China's civil aviation sector has expanded rapidly in the past 16 years, growing by an average of 20.6 percent between 1980 and 1995. It was forecast to grow 14 percent annually through the end of the century.
As of end-1996, Liancheng said China had a total of 317 aircraft leased from countries including the United States, Germany, France and Japan at a cost of a total of $11.8 billion.
The country's air fleet now had 443 aircraft, including the leases, worth a total of $16 billion, Liancheng said.
"By the year 2000, the number of aircraft in the entire industry will reach 1,000 and more," he said.
Liancheng complained that foreign firms still insisted on state bank guarantees for Chinese leasing orders.
He said time had come for aircraft makers to treat the Chinese like other credible clients given China's market reforms, its rapid growth and booming aviation business.
"Our high credibility is the most convincing proof. Chinese airlines' reputation, combined with mortgages on their property should gradually replace bank guarantees," he said.

The reputation of China's airlines has indeed improved since 1994, when the International Airline Passenger Association cited the country as one of the most dangerous places in the world in which to fly after a string of crashes and hijackings.
In the following two years China did not have an aviation disaster. In 1996, its airlines set a record of 29 months, and 2.33 million hours, of safe flying, according to its officials.
Liancheng said China expected to boost air passenger traffic to 100 million travellers and cargo traffic to two million tonnes by 2010 -- nearly a 100 percent rise over 1995 levels.
In 1996, China's airlines flew 55.5 million passengers, up 8.5 percent over a year ago, while air cargo traffic grew more than 13 percent to 1.14 million tonnes.
Chinese plans now flew to 797 routes, 694 of them domestic, and serving 85 international routes including 53 cities in 33 countries -- 38 cities and 19 countries more than in 1990.
Airline industry officials say that on a worldwide scale, China has a long way to go to catch up with the United States, Europe and Japan in terms of passenger and cargo traffic.

By comparison, the world's busiest cargo airport Memphis, base of U.S. express freight carrier Federal Express, handled 167,015 tonnes of cargo in November 1996 alone, according to the Geneva-based Airports Council International (ACI).
China's passenger traffic for the whole of 1996 is also tiny compared to total world traffic of 189.3 million flyers alone in November, including Europe airports which handled 52.9 million.
